questions.q: According to the lesson, where does bias overwhelmingly originate before a model is even trained?
options: In the training data itself, which a learning algorithm then finds and reinforces
In the physical computer hardware running the training job
In the programming language used to write the model's code
In the color scheme of the software's user interface
questions.explain: The lesson states the algorithm doesn't invent bias — it reinforces patterns already present in the training data.

questions.q: What is sampling bias, as described in the lesson, and how does it connect to an earlier lesson?
options: A mismatch between the training population and the population the model is used on — a direct consequence of the completeness dimension from Lesson 8
A bias that only occurs in surveys conducted by phone
An error that occurs only when a dataset is too large
A type of bias that has nothing to do with data quality
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ties sampling bias to the completeness dimension covered in Lesson 8.

questions.q: What is a 'proxy variable,' per the lesson, and what risk does it carry?
options: A stand-in measurement used because the real thing is hard to measure, which may not mean the same thing for everyone
A second copy of the same dataset stored as a backup
A variable that only exists in spreadsheet software
A government-issued identification number
questions.explain: The lesson defines proxy variables and explains measurement bias occurs when the proxy doesn't hold equally for everyone.

questions.q: Why can a model be accurate overall while still being biased against a specific subgroup?
options: The overall accuracy number averages performance across everyone, which can hide meaningfully worse performance for one subgroup
Overall accuracy and subgroup performance are always mathematically identical
Subgroups cannot be measured separately in any dataset
Bias only ever affects a model's training speed, not its accuracy
questions.explain: The lesson explains that an aggregate accuracy score can mask meaningfully worse performance for a specific subgroup underneath it.

questions.q: What does label bias refer to, as introduced in this lesson?
options: Human labelers' own judgments and inconsistencies becoming part of the ground truth a model learns from
A barcode label being printed incorrectly on a physical product
A model's inability to read any text labels at all
A legal requirement to label all AI-generated content
questions.explain: The lesson defines label bias as human judgment and inconsistency entering the ground-truth labels, to be covered further in Lesson 10.
